sections.heading: Types and variables
points: Value types (`int`, `double`, `decimal`, `bool`, `char`, `struct`, `enum`) hold their data directly. Reference types (`string`, `class`, arrays, `object`) hold a reference to an object on the heap.
Use `decimal` for money. `double` is binary floating point and cannot represent many decimal fractions exactly, so rounding errors creep in.
A local variable must be definitely assigned before it is read, otherwise the compiler refuses to build.
`var` lets the compiler infer the type. The variable is still statically typed, it is not dynamic.
`string` is immutable: every 'change' creates a new string. Use `StringBuilder` when building text in a loop.
Nullable reference types (`string?`) and null operators `?.`, `??` and `??=` help you handle missing values safely.

sections.heading: Control flow and operators
points: `if`/`else`, `switch` (statements and expressions), `for`, `foreach`, `while`, `do/while`, plus `break` and `continue`.
Integer division truncates (`7 / 2` is `3`), and `%` gives the remainder.
`==` compares values for value types and, for most reference types, references. `string` overloads `==` to compare content.

sections.heading: Methods
points: A method has a return type, a name and parameters. `void` means no return value.
Overloading means the same method name with different parameter lists.
`ref` and `out` pass arguments by reference. `out` must be assigned by the method. Optional and named arguments make calls shorter and clearer.
Expression-bodied members (`int Double(int x) => x * 2;`) are a compact form for one-line methods.

sections.heading: Object-oriented programming
points: Encapsulation: keep fields `private` and expose behaviour through methods and properties.
Inheritance: a class derives from one base class with `:`. Use `virtual` in the base and `override` in the derived class, and `base` to call the parent.
Polymorphism: a base-type reference can hold a derived object, and the overridden method that runs is chosen at runtime.
Abstraction: `abstract` classes cannot be instantiated and may contain unimplemented members. Interfaces define a contract that a class can implement, and a class can implement many interfaces.
`new` allocates an object on the heap and runs its constructor. Constructors have the class name and no return type.
Access modifiers: `public`, `private`, `protected`, `internal`. Properties use `{ get; set; }`, and `init` allows setting only during construction.

sections.heading: Exceptions and resources
points: `try`/`catch`/`finally`: catch the most specific exception first. `finally` always runs.
Rethrow with `throw;` to preserve the stack trace. `throw ex;` resets it.
Objects that hold resources implement `IDisposable`. Wrap them in a `using` statement so they are released even if an exception occurs.
Custom exceptions derive from `Exception`.

sections.heading: Memory basics
points: Value types usually live on the stack (or inline in their container), reference-type objects live on the heap.
The garbage collector frees heap objects that are no longer reachable. You do not free memory yourself.
Boxing wraps a value type in an object on the heap, and unboxing extracts it. It costs allocations, so avoid it in hot code.

sections.heading: Choosing a collection
points: Array: fixed size, fastest indexed access.
`List<T>`: resizable, indexed access, the default choice.
`Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`: look up a value by key in roughly constant time. Use `TryGetValue` to avoid `KeyNotFoundException`.
`HashSet<T>`: stores unique items and checks membership quickly.
`Queue<T>`: first in, first out. `Stack<T>`: last in, first out.
Generic collections are type safe and avoid boxing, which is why they replaced `ArrayList` and `Hashtable`.

sections.heading: LINQ basics
points: LINQ queries any `IEnumerable<T>`. It has query syntax (`from x in xs where ... select ...`) and method syntax (`xs.Where(...).Select(...)`).
Filtering and projection: `Where`, `Select`, `Distinct`, `Take`, `Skip`.
Ordering: `OrderBy`, `OrderByDescending`, `ThenBy`.
Grouping and joining: `GroupBy`, `Join`.
Aggregation: `Count`, `Sum`, `Average`, `Min`, `Max`. Tests: `Any`, `All`.
`First` and `Single` throw when there is no match. `FirstOrDefault` and `SingleOrDefault` return the default value instead.

sections.heading: Deferred execution
points: Most LINQ operators do not run when you write them. The query runs when you enumerate it, for example with `foreach`, `ToList()` or `Count()`.
Enumerating the same query twice runs it twice, and it sees the data as it is at that moment.
`IQueryable<T>` (used by EF Core) turns the query into SQL, while `IEnumerable<T>` runs it in memory. Calling `ToList()` too early pulls all rows into memory.

sections.heading: Lambdas and delegates
points: A lambda like `x => x > 5` is a short anonymous function.
`Func<T, TResult>` returns a value, `Action<T>` returns nothing, and `Predicate<T>` returns `bool`.
Modifying a collection while looping over it with `foreach` throws an `InvalidOperationException`.

sections.heading: async and await
points: `Task` and `Task<T>` represent work that completes later. `await` pauses the method without blocking the thread.
Use `async` all the way up. Blocking with `.Result` or `.Wait()` can deadlock.
`async void` is only for event handlers, because the caller cannot await it or catch its exceptions.
`Task.WhenAll` runs tasks concurrently and waits for all of them. Pass a `CancellationToken` so long operations can be cancelled.

sections.heading: Generics
points: Generics let you write one class or method for many types while keeping type safety, for example `List<T>`.
Constraints restrict what `T` can be: `where T : class`, `where T : new()`, `where T : IComparable<T>`.

sections.heading: Delegates and events
points: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method. Delegates can be multicast, meaning several methods run when invoked.
An `event` is a delegate that outsiders can only subscribe to or unsubscribe from. They cannot invoke it. This is the observer pattern.

sections.heading: Modern language features
points: `record` types give value-based equality and non-destructive copying with `with`.
Pattern matching (`is`, `switch` expressions) lets you test the shape and value of data concisely.
Tuples and deconstruction return several values without a custom class.
Extension methods add methods to existing types without changing them, and `yield return` builds lazy sequences.

sections.heading: Attributes and reflection
points: Attributes attach metadata to code, such as `[Key]`, `[Required]` or `[HttpGet]`.
Reflection reads that metadata and type information at runtime. Frameworks like EF Core and ASP.NET use it heavily, at some performance cost.

sections.heading: Design principles
points: SOLID: Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion.
Depend on abstractions (interfaces) and inject them, so code is easy to change and to test.
The garbage collector uses generations (0, 1, 2) so short-lived objects are collected cheaply. Use `IDisposable` and `using` for unmanaged resources.

sections.heading: Relational basics
points: Data lives in tables of rows and columns. A primary key uniquely identifies a row, and a foreign key points at a row in another table.
Normalization removes duplicated data by splitting it into related tables.
Constraints protect data: `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK`, `DEFAULT`, `PRIMARY KEY`, `FOREIGN KEY`.

sections.heading: Querying
points: Logical order of a query: `FROM`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, `SELECT`, `ORDER BY`.
`WHERE` filters rows before grouping, and `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation.
Joins: `INNER JOIN` keeps matches only, `LEFT JOIN` keeps every left row, `FULL JOIN` keeps everything.
Aggregates: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`. `DISTINCT` removes duplicates, `TOP` limits rows.
Subqueries and CTEs (`WITH`) break complex queries into steps.

sections.heading: Changing data and structure
points: `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` change rows. Always include a `WHERE` on `UPDATE` and `DELETE`.
`DELETE` removes chosen rows and can be rolled back, `TRUNCATE` empties a table quickly, and `DROP` removes the table itself.
Transactions follow ACID: Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable.
Indexes speed up reads but slow writes. A table has one clustered index.
Views, stored procedures, functions and triggers are T-SQL objects stored in the database.

sections.heading: Entity Framework Core
points: `DbContext` is your session with the database, and each `DbSet<T>` represents a table.
Code-first migrations: change your entity classes, run `dotnet ef migrations add Name`, then `dotnet ef database update`.
EF tracks changes to loaded entities. `SaveChangesAsync()` writes all pending inserts, updates and deletes in one transaction.
`Add`, `Remove` and `FindAsync` work with entities. `FindAsync` looks up by primary key.
`Include` loads related data in the same query (eager loading). Forgetting it leads to missing data or the N+1 query problem.
`AsNoTracking()` makes read-only queries faster.
Relationships are configured with navigation properties, data annotations or the Fluent API in `OnModelCreating`.
EF parameterizes queries, which protects against SQL injection.

sections.heading: Hosting and Program.cs
points: `WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args)` creates the builder. Register services on `builder.Services`, call `builder.Build()`, configure the pipeline on `app`, then `app.Run()`.
Environments (`Development`, `Production`) change behaviour such as error pages and which settings load.

sections.heading: Middleware pipeline
points: A request passes through middleware in the order they are registered. Each one can do work, call the next one, or short-circuit and respond.
Typical order: exception handling, HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, authentication, authorization, endpoints.
Authentication must come before authorization, because you must know who someone is before deciding what they may do.

sections.heading: Dependency injection
points: Services are registered with a lifetime: Transient (new each time), Scoped (one per request) and Singleton (one for the whole app).
`AddDbContext` registers the context as Scoped. Do not inject a Scoped service into a Singleton.
Constructor injection is the normal way to receive services in controllers and services.

sections.heading: Controllers and minimal APIs
points: Controllers use attributes: `[ApiController]`, `[Route]`, `[HttpGet]`, `[HttpPost]`. Minimal APIs use `app.MapGet(...)` and lambdas.
Model binding fills parameters from the route, query string, headers or body (`[FromBody]`).
Data annotations (`[Required]`, `[StringLength]`) validate input, and `[ApiController]` returns 400 automatically for invalid models.
Return helpers: `Ok`, `Created`, `NoContent`, `BadRequest`, `NotFound`, `Unauthorized`.

sections.heading: Configuration
points: Settings come from `appsettings.json`, environment-specific files, environment variables and user-secrets. Later sources override earlier ones.
Keep secrets such as connection strings and API keys out of source control.

sections.heading: REST principles
points: Resources are nouns (`/users`, `/users/5`). The HTTP method is the verb.
`GET` reads and is safe. `POST` creates. `PUT` replaces and is idempotent. `PATCH` changes part of a resource. `DELETE` removes and is idempotent.
REST is stateless: every request carries what the server needs to handle it.
Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 500 Server Error.

sections.heading: DTOs and contracts
points: Use Data Transfer Objects for requests and responses instead of exposing database entities directly.
DTOs stop over-posting (clients setting fields they should not) and keep the database shape private.

sections.heading: Practical API features
points: Pagination, filtering and sorting through query parameters keep responses small.
Return errors in a consistent format, for example `ProblemDetails`.
Version your API so changes do not break existing clients.
Document it with OpenAPI/Swagger.
Rate limiting protects the API from abuse.

sections.heading: Layering and patterns
points: Keep controllers thin: Controller, then Service (business rules), then Repository or DbContext (data access).
The Repository pattern hides data access behind an interface. Unit of Work groups changes into one save.
Dependency inversion plus injection makes each layer easy to test and replace.

sections.heading: Authentication versus authorization
points: Authentication answers 'who are you?'. Authorization answers 'what are you allowed to do?'.
401 means not authenticated. 403 means authenticated but not allowed.

sections.heading: Cookies and tokens
points: Cookie authentication: after sign-in the server sets a signed, encrypted cookie and the browser sends it with each request. `HttpOnly` keeps JavaScript from reading it, `Secure` limits it to HTTPS, and `SameSite` limits cross-site sending.
A JWT has a header, payload and signature. It is signed so it cannot be tampered with, but the payload is only encoded, not secret.
Short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens limit the damage if a token leaks.
One-time login links should use random, unguessable tokens that expire and can be used only once.

sections.heading: Access control in ASP.NET Core
points: `[Authorize]` requires a signed-in user. `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]` requires a role, and policies express more complex rules.
Claims describe the user (id, role). Take the user identity from the cookie or token, never from request data the client controls.

sections.heading: Passwords and secrets
points: Never store passwords in plain text. Hash them with a slow, salted algorithm such as bcrypt, PBKDF2 or Argon2. Hashing is one-way, encryption is not.
Do not commit secrets. Use user-secrets, environment variables or a secret store.

sections.heading: Common attacks and defences
points: SQL injection: use parameterized queries or an ORM.
XSS (cross-site scripting): encode output, avoid `innerHTML` with untrusted data, and use a Content Security Policy.
CSRF: use anti-forgery tokens and `SameSite` cookies.
Always use HTTPS, give users and services the least privilege they need, and validate all input on the server.
OAuth2 lets a user grant an app limited access to an account (like Discord login) without sharing their password.

sections.heading: How language models work
points: A large language model predicts the next token from the text so far. It does not look facts up unless it is given tools or documents.
The context window is how much text the model can consider at once.
Models can hallucinate: produce confident but wrong answers. Output varies between runs, especially with a higher temperature.

sections.heading: Writing good prompts
points: Be specific about the task, the audience, the format you want and the constraints.
Give context and source material, and ask it to cite or quote them.
Examples (few-shot prompting) show the model the pattern you want.
Ask for step-by-step reasoning on complex problems, and iterate: refine the prompt based on the output.

sections.heading: Using AI when coding
points: AI is good for boilerplate, explanations, refactors and test ideas. You are still responsible for the result.
Review everything. Run the compiler and tests rather than trusting the code because it looks right.
Work in small steps and understand each change. Blindly accepting large generated code ('vibe coding') leaves you unable to debug it.
Never paste secrets, keys or private data into a prompt.

sections.heading: RAG and safety
points: Retrieval-Augmented Generation finds relevant text chunks (often with embeddings and vector search) and gives them to the model so answers are grounded and can cite sources.
Prompt injection: text from documents or users can contain instructions. Treat retrieved content as data, not commands.
Consider bias, privacy, licensing and cost (tokens) when using AI in a product.

sections.heading: Why test and what to test
points: Tests catch regressions, document behaviour and let you refactor with confidence.
The testing pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a handful of end-to-end tests.

sections.heading: Unit tests with xUnit
points: `[Fact]` marks a single test. `[Theory]` with `[InlineData]` runs the same test with several inputs.
Arrange, Act, Assert: set up, run the code under test, check the result.
Each test should check one behaviour, be independent of other tests and give the same result every run.
Cover the normal case, boundaries (0, 1, max), empty or null input and error cases. Use `Assert.Equal` and `Assert.Throws`.

sections.heading: Isolating dependencies
points: Depend on interfaces so tests can substitute fakes. Mocking libraries (Moq, NSubstitute) create them.
A stub returns canned data, a mock also verifies it was called, and a fake is a simple working replacement such as an in-memory repository.

sections.heading: Integration, TDD and CI
points: `WebApplicationFactory<T>` starts your API in memory so you can test real HTTP requests.
Test-driven development: write a failing test (red), make it pass (green), then clean up (refactor).
Code coverage shows what ran, not whether the tests are good.
Run tests automatically on every pull request with CI such as GitHub Actions.

sections.heading: HTTP
points: The browser sends a request (method, URL, headers, optional body) and the server returns a response (status code, headers, body).
HTTP is stateless. Cookies and tokens carry state between requests.
Useful headers: `Content-Type`, `Authorization`, `Cookie`, `Set-Cookie`, `Cache-Control`.

sections.heading: HTML
points: Use semantic elements (`header`, `nav`, `main`, `section`, `article`, `footer`) so the page has meaning for browsers and screen readers.
Forms collect input. Every input needs a label, and images need `alt` text.

sections.heading: CSS
points: Selectors choose elements. Specificity decides which rule wins: inline beats id, id beats class, class beats element.
The box model: content, padding, border, margin.
Flexbox lays out items in one dimension and Grid in two. Media queries make layouts responsive.
CSS custom properties (`--color`) let you reuse values.

sections.heading: JavaScript
points: Prefer `const` and `let`. Use `===` to compare without type coercion.
Functions are values. A closure is a function that remembers the variables around it. Arrow functions do not have their own `this`.
Promises and `async`/`await` handle asynchronous work. The event loop runs callbacks after the current code finishes.
Array methods `map`, `filter` and `reduce`, plus destructuring and the spread operator, are used everywhere.
`JSON.stringify` and `JSON.parse` convert between objects and JSON text.

sections.heading: The DOM
points: The DOM is the browser's tree of page elements. Find them with `querySelector`, change them with `textContent` and `classList`.
Events bubble up from the target to its ancestors, which makes event delegation possible.
Avoid putting untrusted data in `innerHTML` because it can run injected scripts (XSS). Use `textContent`.

sections.heading: TypeScript and Angular
points: TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript and compiles to it: interfaces, type aliases, generics, union types, and `unknown` (safer than `any`).
Angular builds apps from components with templates, signals for state, services for shared logic, the router for pages and `HttpClient` for API calls.
